name: Amazon Leo Gen1
status_detail: Production satellites launching since April 2025 and enterprise beta service from 2025, but far short of the interim deployment milestone, which the FCC waived in part with conditions in June 2026.

licensed.note: Reduced from the 3,236 originally authorised by a 2024 orbital parameters modification.

regulatory.scope: Gen1 authorisation: 3,236 NGSO FSS satellites in the first Ku-/Ka-band processing round, in three shells at 590 km / 33 deg (784 satellites, 28 planes), 610 km / 42 deg (1,296 satellites, 36 planes) and 630 km / 51.9 deg (1,156 satellites, 34 planes).
Gen1 orbital parameters modification. Reduced the total number of authorised space stations from 3,236 to 3,232.

Amazon Leo applied on 30 January 2026 to extend the interim milestone by 24 months or, alternatively, to waive it. The Space Bureau granted a limited waiver with conditions: it waived the section 25.161(a)(2) automatic-termination cap and part of section 25.164(b)(2), while temporarily demoting the spectral priority of satellites launched after the July 2026 milestone date until the build rate improves. The 100 per cent milestone of 30 July 2029 was not disturbed and the surety bond obligation was not waived.

shells.label: gen1-s1
shells.code_note: Phasing factor not in the authorisation, and the ABNF makes it mandatory, so no code can be emitted from the primary source alone.

shells.label: gen1-s3
shells.code_note: First deployment phase (578 satellites) targets this shell.

spectrum_detail: Ku-/Ka-band under the first Ku-/Ka-band processing round. V-band added to the Gen1 authorisation on 10 February 2026 under the 2021 V-band processing round grant (see amazon-leo-gen2), subject to the same Gen1 milestone schedule.
isl_detail: Optical inter-satellite links demonstrated on prototype satellites; parameters not published in the filings.

launch.cadence: Amazon contracted the largest commercial launch procurement on record across every provider except SpaceX, which was added later, but the vehicles have not flown at the rate the milestones assume. This is the proximate cause of the June 2026 waiver and the clearest case in the registry of launch capacity, not capital or licensing, being the binding constraint.

name: Amazon Leo Gen2 and Polar
status_detail: Authorised 10 February 2026 in the 2021 V-band processing round. Nothing launched under this authorisation; the first milestone is six years out.

regulatory.scope: Application in the 2021 V-band processing round (cut-off established by Public Notice DA 21-941, 4 August 2021), later amended by SAT-AMD-20250311-00068.

Grant stamp, granting in part, deferring in part, with conditions. Authorises Gen1 operations in the 37.5-42.0 GHz and 42.0-42.5 GHz (space-to-Earth, the latter outside the US and possessions only) and 47.2-52.0, 50.4-51.4 and 51.4-52.4 GHz (Earth-to-space) bands, and authorises the Gen2 system (3,212 satellites) and the Polar system (1,292 satellites) on a milestone schedule separate from Gen1's.

shells.label: gen2-and-polar
shells.code_note: The grant is known to this registry only through its citation in DA 26-553, which gives the satellite counts and milestone dates but not the orbital parameters. The Polar system's defining characteristic is its inclination, which is exactly the field not yet recorded. Left empty rather than inferred.

spectrum_detail: 37.5-42.0 GHz and 42.0-42.5 GHz space-to-Earth (the latter outside the US and possessions only); 47.2-52.0, 50.4-51.4 and 51.4-52.4 GHz Earth-to-space. Granted under the 2021 V-band processing round.

sources.title: FCC Space Bureau, Order, DA 26-553 (Kuiper Systems LLC milestone waiver), paragraph 3 and notes 7-8, which describe the 10 February 2026 V-band grant and its milestone schedule
Dan York (Internet Society), "Beyond Starlink: Understanding the Coming Waves of LEO Satellite Deployments", IRTF SPACE RG, IETF 126, Vienna

discrepancies.registry_value: 4,504 across two systems: Gen2 3,212 and Polar 1,292
discrepancies.note: The family total on the slide (7,736) is right. The breakdown is not: the February 2026 grant covers two distinct systems with their own milestone schedule, not a single increment to Gen1. Widely rounded to "4,500" in the press. Splitting them matters because the Polar system is a different orbital regime serving a different coverage problem.

notes: Provenance gap: this record is built entirely from the description of the 10 February 2026 grant contained in a *later* order (DA 26-553). The grant stamp itself, under ICFS SAT-LOA-20211104-00145 and SAT-AMD-20250311-00068, has not been read. Reading it would supply the orbital parameters for both the Gen2 and Polar systems, which are the main gap in this record. Note the source grading subtlety: DA 26-553 is a primary source, and it is a primary source *for what it says*, which is the counts and the milestone dates. It is not a source for the shell geometry, which it does not discuss. A source's grade does not extend beyond its contents.

name: AST SpaceMobile
status_detail: Fully authorised for 248 satellites as of April 2026, including supplemental coverage from space and direct-to-cell operations, with spectrum leases from AT&T, Verizon and FirstNet granted the same day. A small number of satellites are in orbit.

regulatory.scope: Authorisation and Order granting, with conditions, the application as amended nine times (SAT-AMD-20200727-00088, SAT-AMD-20201028-00126, SAT-AMD-20230717-00172, SAT-AMD-20240311-00053, SAT-MOD-20250612-00145, SAT-AMD-20250718-00181, SAT-AMD-20250903-00248, SAT-MOD-20251205-00370, SAT-AMD-20251211-00379, SAT-MOD-20260121-00037). Authority to deploy 223 additional LEO space stations, for 248 in total, and to perform SCS and direct-to-cell operations plus feeder link and TT&C. Issued jointly by the Space Bureau, Wireless Telecommunications Bureau, Office of Engineering and Technology, and Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau. SB Docket No. 25-201.

shells.label: bb1-520
shells.code_note: The authorisation specifies an apogee of 520 km (+/- 30 km) and a perigee of 515 km (+/- 30 km), with operations permitted down to 425 km. The constellation code carries a single circular altitude and has no field for apogee, perigee or a station-keeping tolerance, so the authorised orbit cannot be expressed without discarding information.

shells.label: bb2-520-6planes
shells.code_note: 22 satellites in 6 planes: not evenly divisible, so the code's requirement that satellites be divisible by planes cannot be met. Apogee 520 km, perigee 515 km. sats_per_plane recorded as the floor; the grant does not state the distribution.

shells.label: fm2-460
shells.code_note: A single satellite at apogee and perigee 460 km (+/- 30 km), inclination 50 deg, under its own modification (SAT-MOD-20251205-00370).

shells.label: main-690-685
shells.code_note: 192 satellites "operating each in 1 plane" at an apogee of 690 km and a perigee of 685 km, inclination 53 deg, deployed at 530 km and raised. One satellite per plane is a degenerate Walker configuration, and the orbit is elliptical. Neither is expressible.

shells.label: polar-685-680
shells.code_note: 28 satellites in 2 planes at apogee 685 km, perigee 680 km, inclination 98.1318 deg. Elliptical, and the inclination is specified to four decimal places, which the code's float syntax can carry but which no other record in this registry needs.

spectrum_detail: V-band feeder links and TT&C in 37.5-42.0 GHz (space-to-Earth), 47.2-50.2 and 50.4-51.4 GHz (Earth-to-space) under the August 2024 grant. Service links are supplemental coverage from space using terrestrial cellular spectrum leased from AT&T and Verizon, plus FirstNet spectrum by agreement; the leases were granted the same day as DA 26-391.

sources.title: FCC, Authorization and Order, DA 26-391 (AST & Science, LLC, ICFS SAT-LOA-20200413-00034 and amendments, Call Sign S3065, SB Docket 25-201)
Dan York (Internet Society), "Beyond Starlink: Understanding the Coming Waves of LEO Satellite Deployments", IRTF SPACE RG, IETF 126, Vienna

discrepancies.note: The largest proportional gap found so far, and in the opposite direction to most: the deck understates by roughly a factor of two and a half. The 248-satellite authorisation was granted on 21 April 2026, three months before the talk. The "~100" figure appears to predate it.

notes: This record is the registry's worked example of orbital geometry that the constellation code cannot express for a reason unrelated to phasing: every authorised shell here is elliptical, with apogee and perigee stated separately and a station-keeping tolerance attached. The code assumes a single circular altitude. Four of the five shells also fail the code's divisibility or plane-count assumptions independently. AST's satellites are physically very large, which is why the constellation size is small relative to its coverage ambition. Recording sat_mass_kg for this system would be valuable and has not been done.

name: Blue Origin Project Sunrise
aka: Blue Origin Orbital Data Center System
status_detail: Application filed 19 March 2026; no grant. NASA filed an objection in May 2026. Nothing launched.

filing.document: Blue Origin application for the Project Sunrise orbital data center system, filed 19 March 2026 (ICFS file number not retrieved)
filing.note: The application is public and its filing date is consistently reported, but its ICFS file number has not been retrieved in this pass. Recorded as a document description so the record still anchors on a specific, findable act.

regulatory.scope: Application for up to 51,600 orbital data centre satellites in sun-synchronous orbits between 500 km and 1,800 km, with between 300 and 1,000 satellites per orbital plane. Ka-band requested for telemetry, tracking and command; user data to move over optical inter-satellite links into Blue Origin's TeraWave network and thence to the ground.

NASA filed an objection to the application. The grounds have not been read; NASA objections to large constellations have historically concerned conjunction risk with science missions and with the ISS.

shells.label: sso-500-1800
shells.code_note: Sun-synchronous orbits from 500 to 1,800 km with 300 to 1,000 satellites per plane. Both the altitude and the per-plane population are ranges, so there is no (T, P, F) triple. Sun-synchronous orbits also carry a local time of the ascending node that the code cannot express. Note the per-plane figure: 1,000 satellites in a single plane is two orders of magnitude beyond anything in the operational shells in this registry, and worth flagging to anyone modelling intra-plane topology.

spectrum_detail: Ka-band for TT&C only. No service spectrum of its own; user traffic is to travel by optical link into TeraWave.
isl_detail: Optical links into Blue Origin's own TeraWave constellation, which is itself only announced and has no filing reference in this registry. The compute system's path to the ground therefore depends on a system whose existence is not yet documented in a docket.

sources.title: GeekWire, "51,600 more satellites? Blue Origin adds another twist to the data center space race with Project Sunrise"
SatNews, "NASA Objects to Blue Origin's Project Sunrise"
Dan York (Internet Society), "Beyond Starlink: Understanding the Coming Waves of LEO Satellite Deployments", IRTF SPACE RG, IETF 126, Vienna

discrepancies.note: Count and date both agree with the reporting. The registry adds only that NASA has objected, which the deck does not mention and which is material to whether the filing becomes an authorisation.

notes: Provenance gap: no primary source, and the ICFS file number has not been retrieved. Reading the application would give the shell structure, the satellite design and the basis for the 51,600 figure, and reading NASA's objection would give the first documented instance in this registry of a federal science agency contesting a constellation filing on operational grounds. Both are worth doing.

name: Blue Origin TeraWave
status_detail: Announced January 2026, with deployment stated to begin Q4 2027. No FCC file number has been retrieved for TeraWave itself, though it is referred to in the Project Sunrise filing as the optical backbone that system depends on.
filing_absent: No filing reference retrieved. TeraWave is described in trade press as an announced constellation and is referenced in Blue Origin's Project Sunrise FCC application as the communications network Sunrise will relay through, but no application or grant for TeraWave itself has been located in this pass. It may well exist; this is a gap in our work, not a statement that none exists.

announced.note: Reported alongside the Project Sunrise filing. The IETF 126 deck gives 5,348, with a breakdown of 5,310 LEO and 128 MEO that sums to 5,438. Three mutually inconsistent figures; see discrepancies.

shells.label: leo-meo
shells.code_note: Multi-orbit, with a LEO majority and a small MEO component. No altitudes, inclinations or plane structure traced.

isl_detail: Optical downlinks reported to provide up to 6 Tbps. TeraWave is the intended optical backbone for Blue Origin's Project Sunrise orbital data centres, which makes the two systems a coupled pair: Sunrise has no independent path to the ground.

launch.cadence: In-house launch on New Glenn, which had flown twice as of the March 2026 Sunrise filing.

sources.title: SpaceNews, "Blue Origin joins the orbital data center race"
Dan York (Internet Society), "Beyond Starlink: Understanding the Coming Waves of LEO Satellite Deployments", IRTF SPACE RG, IETF 126, Vienna

discrepancies.note: The deck's own figures do not reconcile: 5,310 + 128 = 5,438, not 5,348. Trade press reporting the Sunrise filing gives 5,408. Three numbers, no filing, no way to choose between them. Recorded as 5,408 only because that figure appears in reporting tied to a document, and flagged here so the uncertainty is visible rather than averaged away.

notes: Provenance gap: no primary source and no filing reference. Everything here is trade press and a conference slide, and the headline count is disputed three ways. Locating a TeraWave application in ICFS would fix all of it. Recorded despite that because Project Sunrise, which does have a filing, depends on TeraWave for its ground path. A registry that carried Sunrise but not TeraWave would hide the dependency.

name: Cowboy Space Stampede
status_detail: Application filed 14 May 2026. The company states the satellite design is unfinished and that a licence modification will be needed before service, which is unusually explicit about how provisional the filing is.

filing.document: Cowboy Space application for the Stampede orbital data centre constellation, filed 14 May 2026 (ICFS file number not retrieved)
filing.note: The ICFS file number has not been retrieved.

regulatory.scope: Application for up to 20,000 orbital data centre satellites in dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbits in shells between 700 and 1,000 km. The application provides few details because the satellite design is not finished, and states that a licence modification will be required before service. Launches are said to begin in 2028.

shells.label: dawn-dusk-700-1000
shells.code_note: Dawn-dusk sun-synchronous shells between 700 and 1,000 km. Altitude range, no plane structure, and a local time of the ascending node with no representation in the code. The dawn-dusk choice is the whole point of the design, since it maximises solar exposure, and it is precisely the parameter the notation cannot carry.

sources.title: SpaceNews, "Cowboy files plans for up to 20,000 orbital data centers"
Dan York (Internet Society), "Beyond Starlink: Understanding the Coming Waves of LEO Satellite Deployments", IRTF SPACE RG, IETF 126, Vienna

discrepancies.registry_value: 20,000 requested 14 May 2026; launches stated to begin 2028
discrepancies.note: Count agrees, and the registry can fill in the timeline the deck left blank.

notes: Provenance gap: no primary source and no file number. This record is worth keeping in view for a reason beyond its size. The company told the regulator that the satellite design is unfinished and that a modification will be needed before service. That is a filing made to hold a place in a processing round, stated as such, by the applicant. It is the cleanest documented instance in this registry of the mechanism Dan York and Nitinder Mohan discussed at IETF 126: filings as spectrum positioning rather than deployment commitments. Recording it as `filed` and never as `licensed` is exactly the distinction the registry exists to preserve.

name: CTC-1
operator: Institute of Radio Spectrum Utilization and Technological Innovation
status_detail: Advance publication information received by the ITU on 29 December 2025 and published on 17 March 2026. API/A is the earliest and weakest stage of the ITU process: it precedes the coordination request and confers no coordination priority. Nothing launched and no deployment programme identified.

filed.note: Confirmed against the ITU publication itself: the orbit table of BR IFIC 3067 lists 3,660 orbital planes for this notice, and their per-plane populations sum to exactly 96,714.

itu.note: API/A 14285, notice ID 125545446, received 29 December 2025, published in BR IFIC 3067 on 17 March 2026. No coordination request (CR/C) has been filed, so the network is at the first of the three ITU stages.

shells.label: declared-3660-planes
shells.code_note: 3,660 orbital planes in one notice, spanning altitudes from 300 km to 1,280 km and inclinations from 21 to 98.7 degrees. Most planes carry 30 satellites; the 300 km / 88 degree group carries 79. This is not a constellation in the sense the code models: it is a filing that blankets the LEO shell space. 96,714 is not divisible by 3,660, and no single (T, P, F) triple could describe it even if it were.

sources.title: ITU Radiocommunication Bureau, Space Network List (SNL) Part B, filing history for satellite network CTC-1 (notifying administration CHN)
ITU BR IFIC (Space Services) No. 3067, non-GSO notice data for CTC-1 (tables non_geo and orbit of the published database)
SpaceNews, "China files ITU paperwork for megaconstellations totaling nearly 200,000 satellites"
Dan York (Internet Society), "Beyond Starlink: Understanding the Coming Waves of LEO Satellite Deployments", IRTF SPACE RG, IETF 126, Vienna

discrepancies.note: No longer a discrepancy: the deck's figure is exactly right, and this registry can now say so from the ITU publication rather than take it on trust. Retained as an entry because the deck marked the source as "no confirmed official site", and the point of recording it is that the number has since been confirmed. What the deck's "planned" column still cannot convey is the stage: this is advance publication information, the first and weakest of the three ITU steps.

notes: Upgraded from secondary to primary on 2026-07-29 by querying the ITU Space Network List for the filing identity and then reading the declared orbit data out of BR IFIC 3067 directly. See scripts/itu_query.sh, which reproduces both steps. CTC-1 and CTC-2 together account for about 193,000 of the roughly 200,000 satellites in the December 2025 Chinese filing wave, and therefore for a large share of any global aggregate. A reader deciding how much weight to put on a 2.3 million total should know that roughly 8 per cent of it comes from two filings by a single research institute, with a stated purpose that nobody has confirmed. Making that visible is the point of keeping the record.

name: Eutelsat OneWeb
status_detail: First-generation constellation complete and in wholesale service. Authorised by the United Kingdom; US market access granted by the FCC and modified in 2023 from 720 to 716 satellites. A requested expansion to 6,372 satellites was deferred, not granted.

filing.note: The underlying authorisation is British, held by WorldVu Satellites Limited. The file number recorded here is the US market access petition, which is the citable public docket; the UK authorisation itself has not been retrieved. `administration` is the ITU code for the United Kingdom.

licensed.note: Reduced from 720 to 716 in the 2023 modification. This is the figure for which US market access is granted; the UK authorisation is assumed to match but has not been read.

filed.note: OneWeb's modification petition requested an expansion of the system to 6,372 satellites. The FCC granted the reduction to 716 and expressly deferred consideration of the expansion. Under this registry's convention filed is cumulative of everything requested, so the 6,372 stands here and only 716 is licensed.

regulatory.scope: Grant of OneWeb's April 2016 petition for declaratory ruling for US market access for a 720-satellite constellation in 18 near-polar planes with 40 satellites per plane at approximately 1,200 km, 87.9 degrees inclination. The petition triggered the NGSO processing round that Starlink, Telesat and others later joined.

Order and Declaratory Ruling granting in part and deferring in part (with SAT-APL-20210112-00007). Reduces the constellation from 720 to 716 satellites and changes the architecture from 40 satellites in each of 18 planes at 87.9 degrees to 49 satellites in each of 12 planes at 87.9 degrees plus 16 satellites in each of 8 planes at 55 degrees, with no change to operational altitude. Consideration of the requested expansion to 6,372 satellites is deferred.

shells.label: phase1-polar
shells.code_note: Phasing factor not in the order. The altitude is recorded as the "approximate" 1,200 km stated in the FCC's description of the original petition, and the modification states the operational altitude is unchanged.

shells.label: phase1-inclined
shells.code_note: The 55 degree "inclined satellites" added by the 2023 modification. The order does not restate the altitude for this group; 1,200 km is carried over from the statement that operational altitude is unchanged, and is therefore an inference rather than a quoted value.

shells.label: original-18x40
shells.code_note: The configuration authorised in 2017 and superseded in 2023. Retained because it is the configuration the constellation-code draft's example table appears to be approximating, and because the NGSO processing round it triggered was defined against it.

spectrum_detail: 10.7-12.7 GHz (space-to-Earth), 14-14.5 GHz (Earth-to-space), 17.8-18.6 GHz (space-to-Earth), 18.8-19.3 GHz (space-to-Earth), 27.5-29.1 GHz (Earth-to-space), 29.5-30 GHz (Earth-to-space).
isl_detail: No inter-satellite links in the first generation; the architecture is bent-pipe through a dense gateway network.

launch.cadence: Deployment completed after switching launch providers following the 2022 suspension of Soyuz launches.

sources.title: FCC Space Bureau, Order and Declaratory Ruling, DA 23-362 (WorldVu Satellites Limited, petition to modify the US market access grant for the OneWeb Ku- and Ka-band NGSO FSS system, IBFS SAT-MPL-20200526-00062 and SAT-APL-20210112-00007, Call Sign S2963)
draft-piraux-space-constellation-code-02, example table (OneWeb as S:1200:87.9:672/12/11)
Dan York (Internet Society), "Beyond Starlink: Understanding the Coming Waves of LEO Satellite Deployments", IRTF SPACE RG, IETF 126, Vienna

discrepancies.registry_value: 588 satellites in 12 planes at 87.9 deg plus 128 in 8 planes at 55 deg (authorised 2023); previously 720 in 18 planes at 87.9 deg (2017)
discrepancies.note: The constellation-code draft's own example table does not match either authorised configuration. Its 672/12 has the right plane count for the current polar group but the wrong satellite count (672 against 588), and it omits the 55 degree inclined group entirely. Worth correcting in the draft, and a useful illustration of why examples in specifications need the same provenance discipline as registry entries.

The deck's 660 launched is consistent. Its "528 (Next)" refers to Eutelsat Next, an announced successor system that needs its own record and does not yet have one. What neither the deck nor most coverage mentions is the deferred request for 6,372 satellites, which is nearly nine times the authorised constellation and is the single largest unremarked number found in this pass.

notes: Provenance gap: the UK authorisation held by WorldVu Satellites Limited has not been retrieved, so the licensed figure recorded here is strictly the number for which US market access is granted. Eutelsat Next, the announced successor constellation, is not recorded and needs its own record once a filing or a firm figure can be traced.

name: Globalstar C-3
parent: Globalstar, Inc. (acquisition by Amazon.com, Inc. filed with the FCC 26 May 2026; pleading cycle open as of June 2026)
status_detail: Licensed by France and notified to the ITU. US market access is sought through a pending petition for declaratory ruling, not a US licence, so the system has no FCC authorisation. Nothing launched.

filing.document: Petition for Declaratory Ruling Granting Access to the U.S. Market for the Globalstar-C3 MSS System; ITU network AST-NG-C-3
filing.note: Two instruments, deliberately not conflated. The ITU network AST-NG-C-3 is notified by France and is recorded under itu: below. The file number here is the US market access petition, which is what makes the system visible in a searchable national docket. `authority` is "other" because the licensing administration is France and the registry's authority enum has no French satellite regulator entry; the French decision itself has not been retrieved.

licensed.note: The system as the FCC describes it: "48 NGSO satellites, licensed by the Republic of France". This is the operational plan, not the size of the ITU filing that backs it. See discrepancies.

filed.note: Declared in the ITU notification. The orbit table of BR IFIC 3069 lists 401 orbital planes for notice 325500157, and their per-plane populations sum to 6,221. Recorded under filed rather than licensed because the declaration is what was filed with the ITU, not what any regulator has authorised anyone to operate.

regulatory.scope: French authorisation of the Globalstar-C3 MSS system of 48 NGSO satellites, held by Globalstar France SAS. The French decision itself has not been retrieved; this entry records its existence as stated by the FCC.

Petition for declaratory ruling seeking access to the US market for the Globalstar-C3 MSS system. Accepted for filing and placed on public notice (Report No. SAT-01923). Still pending as of June 2026.

Application by Globalstar and Amazon for consent to assign and transfer control of all Globalstar space station, earth station and section 214 authorisations to Amazon. Accepted for filing 4 June 2026; petitions to deny due 6 July 2026.

itu.note: Full filing chain in SNL Part B: API/A 9629 received 20 June 2016 (published WIC 2825, 2 August 2016); CR/C 4149 received the same day (WIC 2837, 24 January 2017), modified three times through September 2022; Resolution 49 due diligence 2422 in 2021; notification Part I-S, Part II-S and Part III-S from December 2021 onward. The most recent act is a Part I-S received 22 August 2025 and published in BR IFIC 3069 on 14 April 2026, notice ID 325500157, which is the one read for the satellite count.

shells.label: declared-401-planes
shells.code_note: 401 orbital planes at 680, 800, 1000, 1400 and 1414 km, at inclinations stepped every two degrees from 60 to 90 plus sun-synchronous cases at 98.1, 98.5, 99.4 and 101.4 degrees, mostly 16 satellites per plane with a few carrying 4 or 1. A single notice covering five altitudes and more than twenty inclinations is not one Walker constellation and cannot be reduced to a (T, P, F) triple. An announced programme from an operator of this size, with no stated constellation size, is a real category and the honest representation of it is absence. Writing a speculative number here would corrupt exactly the aggregate the registry is meant to make trustworthy. Provenance gap: the Google Research post describing the system design has been cited but not read in detail; it would give the cluster geometry and the power and thermal assumptions.

name: Qianfan
parent: Backed by the Shanghai Municipal People's Government; Chinese Academy of Sciences involvement reported
status_detail: Launching production satellites since August 2024; regional service targeted for around 2026 and global service around 2030. Well short of the announced phase targets.
filing_absent: No filing reference has been established for this system. China's national authorisations are not published in a public docket comparable to the FCC's ICFS, and the ITU SNS records for the Chinese administration's filings have not been searched for a network matching this constellation. Unlike starshield, this is a gap in our work rather than a structural limit: a filing very probably exists and can be found.

announced.note: Company build-out target of roughly 15,000 satellites by 2030, in phases of 648 (regional), 1,296 (global) and the remainder. The IETF 126 slide gives 16,000; both figures circulate. No filing has been consulted that substantiates either, so this sits under announced rather than filed.

itu.note: NOT CONFIRMED for this system specifically. China filed with the ITU in late 2025 for frequency and orbital resources covering on the order of 200,000 satellites across roughly 14 constellations. Whether and how much of that filing set covers Qianfan has not been checked against the ITU SNS database. This entry records the existence of the filing wave, not a Qianfan filing identity.

shells.label: phase-1
shells.code_note: Operational altitude around 1,160 km at roughly 85 deg inclination is widely reported, but no plane count, satellites-per-plane or phasing has been traced to a source good enough to record here. Left empty rather than guessed.

providers: China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC)
launch.cadence: Roughly 240 satellites in two years against a stated target of 15,000 by 2030. The implied required rate is the interesting number here.

sources.title: Dan York (Internet Society), "Beyond Starlink: Understanding the Coming Waves of LEO Satellite Deployments", IRTF SPACE RG, IETF 126, Vienna
Wikipedia, "Qianfan"
SpaceNews, "China files ITU paperwork for megaconstellations totaling nearly 200,000 satellites"

discrepancies.note: Both 15,000 and 16,000 circulate widely and neither has been traced to a filing in this revision. Recorded as announced, not filed, precisely because the discrepancy cannot currently be resolved against a document.

notes: Provenance gap: this record has no primary source at all, and that is the point of keeping it in this state rather than filling the fields from press coverage. The primary sources that would fix it are (a) the ITU SNS/SRS records for the Chinese administration's filings covering this system, and (b) any MIIT authorisation document. Neither has been consulted. This record is the registry's worked example of the non-US jurisdiction problem: for FCC-licensed systems the filing, the geometry, the milestones and the spectrum are all in a public docket, and for most others they are not. Any aggregate satellite count that treats a Chinese or Russian figure as equivalent evidence to an FCC grant is comparing unlike things, and the registry should make that visible rather than smooth it over.

name: Rassvet
status_detail: First 16 production satellites launched 23 March 2026 after an experimental phase from 2023. Of the three ITU networks filed in 2022-2023, two were suppressed at the operator's own administration's request in December 2025; only RASSVET-1 remains on file.

filing.note: Anchored on RASSVET-1, the only one of the three networks still on file. RASSVET and RASSVET-2 were suppressed; see itu: below.

launched.note: Includes experimental satellites from 2023 and the 16 production satellites launched 23 March 2026. The deck gives "~21-22".

filed.note: Declared in the first modification of the RASSVET-1 coordination request. The orbit table of BR IFIC 3042 lists 30 planes of 45 satellites at 500 km, 60 degrees, for notice 323520262.

announced.note: Company plan: 292 operational satellites by the end of 2030 out of 383 launched. Russia's Internet Access Infrastructure federal project separately gives 156 in 2026, 292 in 2027 and 318 in 2028. None of these matches the 1,350 declared to the ITU.

itu.note: API/A 13240 and CR/C 5975 both received 10 January 2023; API/B 2286 and CR/D 5024 followed. The coordination request was modified once, received 10 January 2023 and published in BR IFIC 3042 on 18 March 2025. Still on file.

SUPPRESSED. API/A 13109 and CR/C 5774, both originally received 2 June 2022, carry a suppression action received 29 December 2025 and published in BR IFIC 3065 on 17 February 2026. In SNL Part B the ssn_rev code S means suppression.
SUPPRESSED. API/A 13241 and CR/C 5976, originally received 10 January 2023, carry a suppression action received 29 December 2025 and published in BR IFIC 3065 on 17 February 2026.

shells.label: rassvet-1-500
shells.code_note: Phasing factor not in the ITU declaration. Note that the 500 km, 60 degree geometry matches the orbit the March 2026 batch was launched into, which is a rare case in this registry of the filing and the observed deployment agreeing.

launch.cadence: Launching from Vostochny and Plesetsk. About 22 satellites in three years against a 2030 target of 292 operational and an ITU declaration of 1,350.

discrepancies.note: The deck offers two figures without choosing, which is honest. The registry can now add a third that is documented: RASSVET-1's coordination request declares 1,350 satellites. It matches none of the circulating numbers, and it is larger than all of them, which is the usual direction.

discrepancies.claim: Rassvet is scaling up; hundreds more ahead
discrepancies.registry_value: Two of the three Rassvet ITU networks were suppressed in December 2025
discrepancies.note: A finding that no secondary source in this registry mentions. On 29 December 2025 the Russian administration suppressed both API/A and CR/C for RASSVET and for RASSVET-2, published in BR IFIC 3065 in February 2026, three weeks before the first production launch. Suppression is a deliberate act by the notifying administration, not an expiry. It may be consolidation onto RASSVET-1 rather than retreat, and this registry does not claim to know which. What it does record is that the ITU footprint of this system shrank from three networks to one at the moment the press narrative was about expansion.

notes: Provenance upgraded 2026-07-29 from encyclopaedia and press to the ITU filings and publication. See scripts/itu_query.sh. Reporting on this system is heavily coloured by the war in Ukraine and by its dual-use potential, in both directions. The ITU record is the one part of the picture that is neutral and checkable, which is most of why this round of work was worth doing.

name: Reliance Jio LEO constellation
status_detail: IN-SPACe approved the proposal on 17 July 2026, four days before the IETF 126 session, judging it technically sound. The approval enables the Government of India to support the ITU filings and orbital rights the system needs; those filings are not yet made. Nothing launched.

filing.document: IN-SPACe authorisation of the Jio Platforms LEO constellation proposal, 17 July 2026 (docket identifier not retrieved)
filing.note: IN-SPACe does not publish authorisations in a searchable public docket, so the approval is known only through reporting. The ITU filings that would give the system a citable international identity are still to be made, with government support, which is part of what the approval grants.

licensed.note: Reported as "over 1,600". Recorded as licensed on the strength of the IN-SPACe approval, with the caveat that the approval document has not been read.

regulatory.scope: Approval of Jio Platforms' proposal for a sovereign LEO constellation of more than 1,600 satellites, assessed as technically sound and comparable to Starlink and Kuiper. Reported throughput target of 4.5-5 Tbps against Starlink's approved 600 Gbps and Kuiper's proposed 3 Tbps in India. The approval enables Government of India support for the associated ITU filings and orbital rights coordination.

shells.label: jio-leo
shells.code_note: No orbital parameters published.

launch.cadence: No launch provider disclosed. The sovereign framing makes ISRO the presumption, but that is an inference and not recorded as fact.

sources.title: Business Standard, "Reliance Jio gets IN-SPACe approval for 1,600-satellite LEO network"
SpaceNews, "India's Jio lays out sovereign LEO constellation plan ahead of IPO"
Dan York (Internet Society), "Beyond Starlink: Understanding the Coming Waves of LEO Satellite Deployments", IRTF SPACE RG, IETF 126, Vienna

discrepancies.claim: Deployment "next 2-3 years" if approved; announced Jun 19 2026 at AGM
discrepancies.note: The deck's conditional was correct when written and was overtaken four days before the session: IN-SPACe approved the proposal on 17 July 2026. A good argument for a registry with dated `verified` fields over a slide deck.

notes: Provenance gap: no primary source and no citable docket. IN-SPACe authorisations are not published in a form comparable to FCC ICFS. Carlos Martinez-Cagnazzo asked at IETF 126 who the proper authority is when a company files, and Dan York used exactly this system as the example: the Indian space agency approves, then the filing goes to the ITU. This record captures that chain at the moment the first step completed and the second had not yet begun, which makes it a useful teaching case for the draft.

name: SpaceX Orbital Data Center System
status_detail: Application filed 30 January 2026, accepted for filing 4 February 2026. No grant. This single application is the largest contributor by far to every circulating aggregate of planned satellites.

filed.note: The public notice says "up to one million satellites", twice, in those words. It is a ceiling stated in the application, not a deployment plan.

regulatory.scope: Application for authority to launch and operate a new NGSO system of up to one million satellites, the "SpaceX Orbital Data Center system", at altitudes from 500 km to 2,000 km in 30 degree and sun-synchronous inclinations, within orbital shells spanning up to 50 km each. Different satellite hardware versions are planned across shells.
Space Bureau accepts the application for filing and seeks comment.

shells.label: odc-band
shells.code_note: The application describes a *range*, not shells: altitudes from 500 km to 2,000 km, inclinations of 30 degrees and sun-synchronous, within shells spanning up to 50 km each. No plane count, per-plane population or phasing. Sun-synchronous orbits additionally carry a local time of the ascending node, which the constellation code has no field for. Nothing here is expressible as a Walker triple, and a registry that invented one would be inventing the topology.

isl_detail: Optical inter-satellite links are the system's primary communications path. Per the application, the links "will route traffic within the network and to satellites in the Starlink constellation, via its high capacity (petabit) and high reliability laser mesh, which in turn will transmit traffic to authorized earth stations on the ground". The system therefore depends on the Gen1 and Gen2 Starlink authorisations for its ground path, which is a coupling between three separate licences worth noting.
spectrum_detail: Optical for user traffic; RF for telemetry, tracking and command only. The public notice does not state the TT&C bands.

sources.title: FCC Space Bureau, Public Notice DA 26-113, "SpaceX's Application for Orbital Data Centers Accepted for Filing and Comment Sought" (ICFS SAT-LOA-20260108-00016, Call Sign S00798)
Dan York (Internet Society), "Beyond Starlink: Understanding the Coming Waves of LEO Satellite Deployments", IRTF SPACE RG, IETF 126, Vienna

discrepancies.note: The application, as described in the FCC's own acceptance notice, is for "up to one million satellites". The slide's 1,198,120 is 198,120 higher and no source for the difference has been found; it may aggregate a separate filing or a tracker's arithmetic. This matters more than most discrepancies in the registry because this one application accounts for roughly half of the widely quoted 2.3 million aggregate, so a 198,120 error here is about 8 per cent of the headline number.

notes: Reported in the press as connected to the SpaceX/xAI merger. The application itself is for a communications authorisation; the compute payload is not what the FCC is licensing, which is worth remembering when reading the filing as evidence about data-centre capacity. Provenance gap: the application narrative and technical attachment (Attachment A) are cited in DA 26-113 but have not been read directly. They would give the shell structure, the satellite versions and the TT&C bands.

name: SpinLaunch Meridian Space
status_detail: FCC application for roughly 1,200 satellites in Ka-, Ku- and V-band. 280 satellites contracted from Kongsberg NanoAvionics in April 2025. Nothing launched.

filing.document: SpinLaunch application for the Meridian Space constellation (ICFS file number and date not retrieved)
filing.note: The ICFS file number and filing date have not been retrieved.

filed.note: Reported as "about 1,200". The IETF 126 deck gives a precise 1,190, which is plausibly the exact figure in the application; the registry records the sourced approximation rather than adopting a precise number it cannot trace.

announced.note: Satellites contracted from Kongsberg NanoAvionics for EUR 122.5m. A manufacturing commitment, not a regulatory figure, and much smaller than the filing.

regulatory.scope: Application to deploy about 1,200 satellites operating in Ka-, Ku- and V-band, at 830 km in an arrangement giving fixed ground tracks rather than precessing ones, so that ground equipment need track in only one dimension. Enterprise and government market rather than consumer.

shells.label: repeating-ground-track-830
shells.code_note: A repeating-ground-track constellation, chosen so that satellite passes recur over fixed points and ground antennas can track in one dimension. The code can express the altitude but has no way to state that the orbits are selected for ground-track repetition, which is the design's defining property and constrains altitude and inclination jointly. Plane count and per-plane population not published.

launch.cadence: The company's kinetic launch system is still in development. The constellation and the launch method are two independent bets, and the deck is right to note that the second is unproven.

sources.title: SpaceNews, "SpinLaunch announces plans for broadband satellite constellation"
Dan York (Internet Society), "Beyond Starlink: Understanding the Coming Waves of LEO Satellite Deployments", IRTF SPACE RG, IETF 126, Vienna

discrepancies.note: The deck's 1,190 is more precise than anything this registry can source and is very likely the exact figure in the application. Recorded as a discrepancy not because the deck is wrong but because the registry cannot yet confirm it, and adopting a precise unsourced number would be exactly the laundering the grading rules exist to prevent. Reading the application would let 1,190 replace "about 1,200" with a primary source behind it.

notes: Provenance gap: no primary source, no file number, no filing date. Worth noting for anyone modelling this system: repeating ground tracks are unusual among the constellations in this registry and change the contact pattern seen by a fixed ground station substantially. It is a good test case for the ground-station elements added in draft-piraux-space-constellation-code-02.

name: Starcloud
status_detail: One demonstrator on orbit (Starcloud-1, November 2025). The 88,000-satellite system is an FCC application accepted for filing in March 2026; no grant.

launched.note: Starcloud-1, a 60 kg demonstrator carrying an NVIDIA H100, launched 2 November 2025. A second demonstrator was reported as planned for October 2026.

filed.note: Requested in the application; nothing granted, so the whole figure is filed and none of it licensed.

regulatory.scope: Application to operate up to 88,000 orbital data centre satellites in a select set of narrow orbital shells between 600 and 850 km, each up to 50 km thick, in dusk-dawn sun-synchronous orbits. Requests Ka-band spectrum for telemetry, tracking and command on a non-interference basis only; bulk data movement is to rely on optical inter-satellite links to third-party broadband constellations. Accepted for filing 13 March 2026.

shells.label: proposed-sso-band
shells.code_note: The application describes a *band* of dusk-dawn sun-synchronous shells between 600 and 850 km, each up to 50 km thick, without a stated plane count, satellites-per-plane or phasing. Sun-synchronous orbits also require an altitude-dependent inclination that the code carries but does not constrain, and the local-time-of-ascending-node that makes an orbit "dusk-dawn" has no representation in the code at all. Nothing here is expressible as a Walker triple.

spectrum_detail: Ka-band requested for TT&C on a non-interference basis. No service spectrum of its own: user data is to move over optical inter-satellite links to Starlink, Amazon Leo and Blue Origin TeraWave.
isl_detail: External dependency. The system as filed has no independent path to the ground for bulk data and relies on crosslinks into constellations operated by other companies, none of which has published an interconnection interface. This is a governance and interoperability question for the group as much as a technical one.

sources.title: SpaceNews, "Starcloud files plans for 88,000-satellite constellation" (reports ICFS SAT-LOA-20260202-00073, filed 2 February 2026, accepted for filing 13 March 2026)
Dan York (Internet Society), "Beyond Starlink: Understanding the Coming Waves of LEO Satellite Deployments", IRTF SPACE RG, IETF 126, Vienna

discrepancies.note: The figure agrees with the application as reported. The disagreement is about the axis, not the number: an accepted-for-filing application establishes a place in a processing round, not an authorisation. This record therefore contributes 88,000 to counts.filed and nothing to counts.licensed.

notes: Provenance gap: this record has no primary source. Everything except the demonstrator launch rests on one trade-press report of the FCC application. The application itself (ICFS SAT-LOA-20260202-00073) is public and should be read; the accepted-for-filing public notice would also be a primary source for the date. Until then every number here is secondary and the record should be read as such. Kept in the registry despite the weak provenance because orbital data centre filings are a large and fast-growing share of the aggregate satellite count, and because this system as filed depends entirely on other operators' optical crosslinks - which is exactly the kind of coupling the group should be able to see.

name: Starlink Gen1
status_detail: Fully deployed and in commercial service. The shells recorded here are the authorised configuration after the April 2021 third modification.

filed.note: The third modification requested, and the Commission granted, a reduction from 4,409 to 4,408. This is the rare case where the filed figure exceeds the licensed figure because the operator asked for less, not because the regulator granted less.

regulatory.scope: Original Gen1 authorisation for the Ku-/Ka-band NGSO system. Not read for this record; cited as it appears in DA 26-113.

Third modification. Reduced the constellation from 4,409 to 4,408 satellites and moved 2,814 satellites from the 1,100-1,300 km range to the 540-570 km range, giving the five-shell configuration recorded below.
Fourth modification. Not read for this record; cited as it appears in DA 26-113. The authorised geometry may have moved since FCC 21-48.
"Swarm modification". Not read for this record; cited as it appears in DA 26-113.

itu.note: Notified by NORWAY, not by the United States. Part I-S received 1 October 2025, published in BR IFIC 3062 on 6 January 2026, notice ID 125500188: 118 planes totalling 1,312 satellites, at 540 km / 53.2 deg (72 planes carrying one satellite each), 560 km / 97.6 deg (6 planes of 58 and 4 of 43) and 570 km / 70 deg (36 planes of 20).

Part I-S, notice ID 125500189: 72 planes of 22 satellites at 550 km, 53 degrees. This is exactly the gen1-s1 shell below, which is the clearest correspondence in the registry between an FCC authorisation and an ITU notification.

API/A 9509 and CR/C 3739 received in 2014, the coordination request modified seven times through 2023, notification Part I-S from 2020 with one suppressed in February 2022, Part III-S in 2024 and 2025, and a further Part I-S received 27 April 2026 published in BR IFIC 3076 on 21 July 2026. Satellite counts for this network were not read.

code_assumptions.basis: Not stated in FCC 21-48, which gives only altitude, inclination, plane count and satellites per plane. F=39 is the value in the example table of draft-piraux-space-constellation-code and in the LEO networking literature it draws on.
Inferred from a 53 deg inclination with uniform plane spacing. The filing does not use Walker terminology.

shells.label: gen1-s2
shells.code_note: Phasing factor not published, and no literature value to borrow as there is for gen1-s1. No code emitted rather than a guessed one.

shells.label: gen1-s5
shells.code_note: Same altitude and inclination as gen1-s4. The two are distinct plane groups within one physical shell; the code can only express them as two "+"-joined shells, which loses the fact that they share a shell. 58 and 43 satellites per plane in 6 and 4 planes respectively is also not a Walker pattern in any useful sense.

spectrum_detail: Ku- and Ka-band under the Gen1 authorisation. V-band capability was later folded into the Gen2 licence rather than a separate constellation.
isl_detail: Optical inter-satellite links from the v1.5 satellite onwards. DA 26-113 describes the result as a "high capacity (petabit) and high reliability laser mesh". Degree and per-link capacity are not in the filings.

sources.title: ITU Radiocommunication Bureau, Space Network List (SNL) Part B, filing histories for satellite networks STEAM-1 and STEAM-2 (notifying administration NOR)
ITU BR IFIC (Space Services) No. 3062, non-GSO notice data for STEAM-2 (notice ID 125500188) and STEAM-2B (notice ID 125500189)
FCC, Memorandum Opinion, Order and Authorization, FCC 21-48 (SpaceX Gen1 third modification, ICFS SAT-MOD-20200417-00037)
FCC Space Bureau, Public Notice DA 26-113, "SpaceX's application for Orbital Data Centers accepted for filing" (cites the Gen1 authorisation and its later modifications)
draft-piraux-space-constellation-code-02, example table (Starlink shell 1 as D:550:53:1584/72/39)

notes: The ITU networks behind Starlink are notified by Norway, not the United States. SpaceX holds a US licence from the FCC and the international filings that carry its spectrum are made by the Norwegian administration under the names STEAM-1, STEAM-2 and STEAM-2B. Nothing improper about that, and it is common practice, but it means a reader looking for Starlink under "USA" in ITU records will not find it, and any jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction tally built from ITU data will attribute the largest constellation in orbit to Norway. This is the single most consequential thing found in the ITU pass. Provenance gap: two later modifications (SAT-MOD-20230215-00036, granted 2024-08-16, and SAT-MOD-20241104-00251, granted 2025-03-17) are recorded from a citation in DA 26-113 but have not been read. The authorised geometry may have changed since FCC 21-48, so the shells here are the 2021 configuration and are marked as such by their src. counts.launched is deliberately empty on this record: launch reporting does not distinguish Gen1 from Gen2 spacecraft, so a per-authorisation launched figure cannot be sourced. The family-level figure is on starlink-gen2.

name: Starlink Gen2
status_detail: Deploying under a partial grant. Authorised for 15,000 of the 29,988 satellites requested; the Commission has expressly deferred action on the remainder. Carries the direct-to-cell (supplemental coverage from space) service.

launched.note: Family-level figure: cumulative Starlink launches across Gen1 and Gen2, including deorbited and failed spacecraft. Launch reporting does not split the two authorisations, so this cannot be attributed to Gen2 alone. Recorded here rather than duplicated on starlink-gen1.

filed.note: SpaceX's preferred configuration as applied for: 29,988 satellites at altitudes from 340 km to 614 km. 14,988 of these remain deferred.

regulatory.scope: Gen2 application, as amended by SAT-AMD-20210818-00105. 29,988 satellites at altitudes from 340 km to 614 km.
First partial grant: 7,500 satellites at 525 km / 53 deg, 530 km / 43 deg and 535 km / 33 deg, roughly a quarter of the request. Action on the remainder deferred.

Authorisation and Order on the Gen2 upgrade modification and amendment (SAT-MOD-20241011-00224, SAT-AMD-20241017-00228). Authorises a second tranche of 7,500 satellites for a total of 15,000; upgrades the satellite form factor; adds Ku-, Ka-, V- and W-band frequencies and MSS as well as FSS in certain bands; adds orbital shells and lowers the satellites at 525, 530 and 535 km into new shells; permits flexible deployment across authorised shells. Requests for MSS outside the US in 1429-2690 MHz and for 20.2-21.2 and 30.0-31.0 GHz, and for satellites beyond 15,000, are deferred.

shells.label: gen2-first-grant
shells.code_note: The December 2022 partial grant authorised 7,500 satellites across three shells at 525 km / 53 deg, 530 km / 43 deg and 535 km / 33 deg without stating a plane count or per-plane population, so no (T, P, F) triple exists. DA 26-36 subsequently authorised lowering these satellites into the 475-485 km shells.

shells.label: gen2-lower-72x144
shells.code_note: Applies to the shells centred at 340 km / 53 deg, 345 km / 48 deg, 350 km / 38 deg, 355 km / 43 deg and 365 km / 28 or 32 deg. DA 26-36 authorises up to 72 planes per shell with up to 144 satellites per plane, and separately permits SpaceX to "deploy satellites flexibly across authorized orbital shells to meet customer demands". There is no single (T, P, F) triple for any of these shells, and no fixed allocation of the 15,000 satellites among them: the licence describes a feasible set.

shells.label: gen2-mid-56x120
shells.code_note: Applies to the shells centred at 480 km / 53 deg and 485 km / 43 deg. Up to 56 planes per shell with up to 120 satellites per plane.

shells.label: gen2-other-authorised
shells.code_note: DA 26-36 also authorises shells at 360 km / 96.9 deg and 475 km / 28 or 32 deg, and continued operation at 525 km / 53 deg, 530 km / 43 deg and 535 km / 33 deg pending lowering. The order's plane/per-plane footnote does not cover these, so even the envelope is unstated. The 365 km and 475 km inclinations are themselves conditional: 32 deg if the FAA permits Starship launches from Boca Chica at that inclination, 28 deg otherwise.

spectrum_detail: Ku-, Ka-, V- and W-band per DA 26-36, plus 1980-2000 MHz and 2000-2020 MHz (Earth-to-space) and 2180-2200 MHz (space-to-Earth) outside the United States for up to 7,500 satellites. Requests for 20.2-21.2 GHz and 30.0-31.0 GHz were deferred.
isl_detail: Optical inter-satellite links on all Gen2 satellites, forming the laser mesh that DA 26-113 describes as petabit-capacity. Not specified in the grant.

sources.title: FCC, Order and Authorization, FCC 22-91 (SpaceX Gen2 NGSO system, first partial grant, ICFS SAT-LOA-20200526-00055 and SAT-AMD-20210818-00105)
FCC Space Bureau, Authorization and Order, DA 26-36 (SpaceX Gen2 upgrade modification and second tranche of 7,500 satellites)
Dan York (Internet Society), "Beyond Starlink: Understanding the Coming Waves of LEO Satellite Deployments", IRTF SPACE RG, IETF 126, Vienna

discrepancies.registry_value: Gen1 4,408 licensed; Gen2 15,000 licensed of 29,988 filed. Family totals: 19,408 licensed, 34,396 filed.
discrepancies.note: The slide aggregates the Gen1 authorisation with the full Gen2 *request* rather than the Gen2 grant, and presents the result in a column labelled "satellites planned". 4,408 + 29,988 = 34,396, which is 468 short of the slide figure; the residual is unexplained. As of DA 26-36 the FCC has authorised 15,000 Gen2 satellites and expressly deferred action on the remaining 14,988.

notes: The ITU networks behind Starlink (STEAM-1, STEAM-2, STEAM-2B) are notified by Norway, not the United States; the shells declared in the most recent STEAM-2 notification match the Gen1 authorisation rather than this one, so the ITU detail is recorded on starlink-gen1. No ITU network has yet been identified that corresponds specifically to the Gen2 authorisation, which is itself worth resolving. This record is the registry's worked example of an envelope authorisation. Three of its four shell entries are geometry_kind envelope or unknown and emit no constellation code, because DA 26-36 bounds the geometry rather than fixing it and lets SpaceX redistribute satellites between shells. Any simulator that wants a concrete Gen2 topology must choose one point in that feasible set, and should say which.

name: Starlink Gen3
status_detail: Application filed 6 July 2026; no grant. Nothing launched under this authorisation. Deployment is predicated on Starship reaching operational cadence at roughly 2,000 kg per satellite.

regulatory.scope: Application for up to 100,000 third-generation satellites in two groups of very low Earth orbit shells, reported as 323-327.5 km and 473-477.5 km, using the Ku-, Ka-, V- and E-band spectrum granted for Gen2 plus new requests in W- and D-band between 92 and 275 GHz.

shells.label: gen3-vleo-323
shells.code_note: Reported altitude band 323-327.5 km. No inclination, plane count or per-plane population has been traced to a source good enough to record.

shells.label: gen3-vleo-473
shells.code_note: Reported altitude band 473-477.5 km. Geometry otherwise unknown.

spectrum_detail: Reported as reusing the Ku/Ka/V/E-band spectrum granted for Gen2, plus greenfield W- and D-band requests between 92 and 275 GHz. Not verified against the application.

launch.cadence: At roughly 2,000 kg per satellite, 100,000 satellites is on the order of 200,000 tonnes to orbit. The feasibility question is entirely a launch question.

notes: Provenance gap: this record has no primary source. The file number, satellite count, altitude bands and spectrum all come from trade press. The application is public in ICFS and should be read; doing so would also settle whether the request is for a genuinely new system or an amendment of the Gen2 authorisation, which changes how the 100,000 should be aggregated.

name: Starshield
status_detail: Satellites are launching regularly on dedicated NRO missions, but the system has no public authorisation, no published constellation size and no published geometry. Status is inferred from launch reporting alone.
filing_absent: No public FCC or ITU filing identifies this system. It is procured and operated under US government contracts, principally for the National Reconnaissance Office's proliferated architecture, and US federal government spectrum use is coordinated through NTIA rather than licensed by the FCC, so no ICFS docket exists to point at. Everything in this record therefore rests on launch reporting and catalogue observation. This is a structural provenance limit, not an oversight, and it applies to classified systems in every jurisdiction.

announced.note: Recorded as announced rather than filed or licensed because no filing has been identified that states a constellation size. The figure is widely reported but not traceable to a document.

isl_detail: Reported to use the same optical inter-satellite link hardware as Starlink and to interoperate with the Starlink laser mesh. Not verifiable from a public document.

sources.title: Dan York (Internet Society), "Beyond Starlink: Understanding the Coming Waves of LEO Satellite Deployments", IRTF SPACE RG, IETF 126, Vienna

notes: Kept in the registry with almost every field empty on purpose. A government constellation of this size is a real consumer of orbital shells and spectrum and a real contributor to conjunction and coordination load, and omitting it because it is undocumented would understate the picture in exactly the direction that is hardest to notice. What the record contributes is the fact, stated in filing_absent, that no public filing exists. Possible future primary sources: the UN Register of Objects Launched into Outer Space (treaty-registry) gives launch-by-launch registrations with orbital parameters, and NTIA spectrum certification records are partially public. Neither has been checked.

name: Telesat Lightspeed
status_detail: Authorised by ISED in Canada, with US market access granted separately by the FCC. 198 satellites contracted from MDA in August 2023, down from an earlier 298. Telesat has stated it will not meet the current ISED milestones and intends to seek an amendment. Nothing launched.

filing.document: ISED NGSO authorisation for the Telesat Lightspeed constellation (identifier not retrieved)
filing.note: The Canadian authorisation is referenced in Telesat's own annual report but its docket identifier has not been retrieved, and ISED does not publish satellite authorisations in a searchable docket comparable to the FCC's ICFS. The FCC market access grant is a separate act and is recorded under regulatory: below.

announced.note: Satellites contracted from MDA, reduced from an earlier 298. Recorded as announced rather than licensed because the number authorised by ISED has not been retrieved and may differ from the number ordered.

regulatory.scope: US market access for the Telesat Canada NGSO constellation, granted by declaratory ruling. Date and document number not retrieved; a separate petition covers Telesat's V-band constellation.
Canadian authorisation with deployment milestones that Telesat has stated it will not meet and intends to seek to amend.

spectrum_detail: Ka-band primary, with a separate V-band constellation petition at the FCC. Mil-Ka defence spectrum reported as being added. Ranges not recorded.

discrepancies.note: The deck records three candidate figures with question marks, which is an honest way to present an unresolved number and worth saying so. This registry can partly resolve it: 198 is the number contracted from MDA in August 2023, down from an earlier plan of 298 (probably the "300"). The 1,600 appears to be a much earlier ambition. What none of these is, yet, is an authorised figure.

notes: Provenance gap: this record has no usable primary source for its counts. The FCC market access grant is cited by landing page rather than by document number and has not been read, and the ISED authorisation has not been located at all. This record is the registry's worked example of the non-US-but-Western jurisdiction problem, which sits between the FCC case and the Chinese case: the authorisation certainly exists and is not secret, but it is not published in a form that can be cited, so the best available evidence is the operator's own reporting. Any contributor with ISED experience could close this quickly.
